Lighter-weight and higher-energy-density batteries, such as lithium-sulfur (Li-S) or solid-state lithium batteries with lithium anodes, could improve capabilities for UAVs, high- altitude pseudo-satellites, autonomous underwater vehicles, and heavy road vehicles (Dorfler et al. 2020). Researchers are continuing to improve the capacity, performance, and cost- competitiveness of these advanced battery options, with commercialization expected by 2030 for Li-S, sodium-ion batteries, and silicon and silicon-carbon anodes, according to NLR experts. DOW might want to partner with others to fund research of mutual interest. For example, because tidal power commercialization is expected to take at least another decade due to high costs (Cart 2023), DOW might partner with allied leaders in this area, including the United Kingdom, France, Canada, Australia, Portugal, and South Korea. South Korea’s 254-megawatt (MW) facility is the largest to date. To counter the risks related to cyber and kinetic attacks and natural disasters, more research could be developed to address energy infrastructure vulnerabilities supporting critical missions or geographies. One existing effort at NLR identifies tools for informing cybersecurity solutions for emerging energy technologies and evolving threats. Continued growth in this research area could yield mitigations that are applicable in the defense space as DOW technology adoption evolves (DOE CESER 2024). Actions to mitigate the risks of adversaries leapfrogging U.S. advancements in technologies that are critical to DOW operations include implementing robust intellectual property protection strategies where possible, ensuring secure development practices, applying stringent cybersecurity measures, and facilitating international cooperation to safeguard proprietary technologies from theft or unauthorized access. 23 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. 6.9 Partnerships and Working Groups DOW can mitigate some risks by expanding relationships with international partners, local utilities, and communities surrounding DOW installations. DOW could also leverage working groups. For example, DOW could participate in the Alaska Hydrogen Working Group, which is an informal group of stakeholders who are interested in following developments related to hydrogen technologies and in providing inputs related to the proposed use and future deployment in the state of Alaska (UAF n.d.). DOW’s involvement could raise certain DOW-specific hydrogen energy needs to broaden commercial hydrogen development efforts. Expanding international partnerships beyond interoperability to the development of new technologies could help keep DOW, allies, and partners ahead of adversaries. For example, DOW might want to partner with the United Kingdom, France, Canada, and Portugal to explore defense applications of wave and tidal energy advancements. In 2023, the global installed capacity of tidal energy was 600 MW; leading projects are located in the United Kingdom, France, and Canada. China and India are also starting pilot tidal projects. Additionally, multiple interviewees pointed to the strategic advantage in building and maintaining relationships with other nations, including through building infrastructure, to increase the likelihood of access to ports and materials and to influence energy infrastructure development in those countries, which is a strategy China has successfully used in countries such as the Philippines.
